case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Amendment permits Congress to categorically bar firearm possession by a person who qualifies as an “unlawful user” of controlled substances under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), even when the person is not shown to be intoxicated at the moment of possession, and whether that prohibition is constitutional as applied to Ali Danial Hemani under Bruen’s history-and-tradition test.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (prohibiting firearm possession by anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”) and the Second Amendment (as interpreted through New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen’s historical-analogue framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because history and tradition support temporarily disarming persons whose ongoing condition or status makes firearm possession unusually dangerous—particularly through analogues such as historical regulations disarming or restricting firearm use by the intoxicated and by “habitual drunkards.” The government contends the Fifth Circuit’s ruling effectively invalidates most applications of a frequently used federal statute, deepens a circuit split, and misapplies Bruen by demanding an overly narrow founding-era twin rather than a relevantly similar historical tradition addressing the same risk (armed impairment/addiction and heightened danger).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to him because the relevant historical tradition supports, at most, restrictions on carrying/using guns while actively intoxicated (or for truly incapacitated ‘habitual drunkards’), not a broad status-based prohibition triggered by regular use of a substance Congress has labeled ‘controlled.’ He maintains that Bruen requires a closer analogue than the government offers, that ‘unlawful user’ sweeps in many ordinary, non-dangerous users without individualized dangerousness or contemporaneous impairment, and that the government’s approach risks turning an as-applied challenge into de facto approval of a categorical ban lacking historical support.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch make the best point that many historical analogues target carrying or firing while actually intoxicated and that § 922(g)(3) risks becoming a broad, status-based disability. But Bruen, as clarified by Rahimi (as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes), does not require a founding-era twin; it permits analogous reasoning where the law’s why/how align, and the historical tradition of intoxication and habitual-drunkard regulations supports temporarily separating firearms from persons whose ongoing substance abuse predictably impairs judgment. I would answer Justice Gorsuch’s process concern by avoiding any free-floating “dangerousness” standard and by limiting our holding to an as-applied record showing current, regular unlawful use close in time to possession—rejecting the Fifth Circuit’s near-identical-analogue demand without endorsing § 922(g)(3) in more attenuated cases. On that narrow ground, the opposing insistence on intoxication-at-possession mini-trials overreads our methodology and would undermine workable enforcement in a way our tradition does not compel.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito are right that Bruen and Rahimi do not demand a “historical twin,” but they still require a relevantly similar “why” and “how,” and the Government’s analogues do not match § 922(g)(3)’s categorical, criminal disarmament based on a broad modern status label. The Founding-era laws Roberts, Kavanaugh, and Barrett invoke chiefly regulated carrying or firing while actually intoxicated (and only rarely addressed extreme “habitual drunkards”), whereas § 922(g)(3) imposes an ongoing possession ban without proof of contemporaneous impairment or any historically grounded, surety-like process—precisely the kind of procedural mechanism Rahimi highlighted as part of our tradition. Administrability cannot supply the missing historical fit; under an original public-meaning approach, we may not expand targeted intoxication restrictions into a sweeping disability keyed to Congress’s controlled-substance classifications and prosecutorial proof of “use.” Accordingly, the Government has not carried its burden under Bruen/Rahimi as applied to Hemani.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that founding-era analogues often targeted being armed while actually intoxicated or required some process (surety-type mechanisms), and that § 922(g)(3) risks looking like a status offense keyed to modern drug schedules. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain, Bruen and Rahimi reject a “historical twin” requirement and instead ask whether the law is relevantly similar in why/how; the tradition is disarming those whose condition makes gun possession unusually dangerous, and § 922(g)(3) is temporary and conduct-linked (current unlawful use), not a lifetime class-wide ban. Rahimi also undercuts the premise that only individualized, judicial dangerousness findings can justify disarmament—categorical rules grounded in historically recognized risk principles are permissible, and requiring intoxication-at-possession mini-trials would largely defeat a prophylactic measure that history did not demand. I would, however, accept Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing move: uphold as applied where the record shows ongoing unlawful use close in time to possession, leaving harder edge cases for later.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s insistence on contemporaneous-intoxication proof or individualized judicial findings has force as a fair-notice and fit objection, but it reads Bruen/Rahimi as demanding a procedural mechanism (surety-like process) rather than the relevantly similar “why/how” inquiry those cases actually prescribe. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 922(g)(3) is temporally bounded by the present-tense “is an unlawful user,” and—when the record shows ongoing, regular use close in time to possession—it functions as a condition-linked, prophylactic restriction akin in purpose to historical intoxication and habitual-drunkard measures aimed at preventing predictable impairment-related misuse. Justice Thomas is right to warn against a broad, modern status disability keyed to malleable drug schedules, which is why I would keep the holding narrow and leave room for as-applied challenges where “ongoing use” is attenuated or poorly proved. But on this record, and under Rahimi’s acceptance of categorical, historically anchored risk-based disarmament without a founding-era twin, the Government has met its burden as applied to Hemani.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best objection: the historical record most clearly supports regulation of being armed while actually intoxicated, or narrow “habitual drunkard” measures, not a categorical federal ban keyed to “unlawful user” status and modern controlled-substance schedules. But under Bruen as clarified by Rahimi (which Justice Kavanaugh and the Chief rightly emphasize), we ask whether the modern law is relevantly similar in why/how, and the why here is impairment-linked risk from ongoing substance abuse; the how is a temporary, condition-linked restriction that tracks the period of current unlawful use rather than a free-floating dangerousness standard. I am not persuaded by Justice Gorsuch’s process point because Rahimi does not make surety-like individualized adjudication a prerequisite in every disarmament context, and requiring proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession—Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern—would effectively disable any prophylactic regulation despite a historical tradition of preventing foreseeable harms tied to intoxication. The textual narrowing in “is an unlawful user of” supplies the limiting principle Thomas seeks, keeping the rule tethered to current, regular unlawful use close in time to possession, and that is sufficient to uphold the statute as applied here while leaving harder, attenuated-use cases for another day.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern and Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Rahimi’s “relevantly similar” framing do not, for me, supply the missing historical analogue: the cited tradition addresses being armed while actually intoxicated or, at most, narrowly defined habitual drunkenness, not § 922(g)(3)’s categorical possession ban keyed to “unlawful user” status. Rahimi matters, but it emphasizes that the historical “how” typically involved temporally limited restraints following some concrete, historically grounded mechanism (surety-like process or comparable finding of threat), whereas § 922(g)(3) turns on modern controlled-substance classifications and a prosecutor’s proof of “use,” not an adjudicated showing of dangerousness. Justice Alito’s point that the disability is “temporary” mitigates severity but does not cure the Bruen fit problem; a time-limited status ban still needs a Founding-era analogue in why/how, and the Government’s proposed generality level risks converting targeted intoxication rules into a free-floating dangerousness principle. Given the criminal setting, fair-notice and lenity concerns reinforce that we should not stretch history to validate a broad disarmament category absent a closer fit, at least as applied to Hemani.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that the historical analogues most directly prohibit carrying/shooting while actually intoxicated (and occasionally address “habitual drunkards”), whereas § 922(g)(3) can look like a broader, status-based possession ban without contemporaneous-impairment proof or individualized process. But under Bruen as clarified by Rahimi, we do not demand a Founding-era twin mechanism; we ask whether the modern law is relevantly similar in why and how, and a temporary disarmament tied to ongoing unlawful use fits the historically rooted principle of preventing foreseeable misuse by those whose substance condition predictably impairs judgment. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that requiring intoxication-at-possession mini-trials (or case-by-case judicial dangerousness findings) would be historically unnecessary and practically unadministrable for a prophylactic, time-limited rule, and Rahimi undermines the notion that only individualized findings can support disarmament. On a narrow as-applied record showing current, regular unlawful use close in time to possession, § 922(g)(3) remains sufficiently bounded to avoid the unmoored, lifetime status disability Justice Thomas warns against.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is that the most direct Founding-era analogues target being armed while actually intoxicated and often used process (e.g., surety-like mechanisms), whereas § 922(g)(3) is a categorical criminal disability keyed to “unlawful user” status. But under Bruen as clarified by Rahimi—emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh—the inquiry is relevant similarity in “why” and “how,” not a demand for a historical twin: the historical tradition supports temporarily separating arms from persons whose ongoing substance abuse predictably impairs judgment and heightens risk, and § 922(g)(3)’s present-tense “is an unlawful user” limits it to current, regular unlawful use rather than a permanent status ban. I do not read Rahimi to constitutionalize individualized judicial dangerousness findings in every case; it recognizes categorical restrictions when grounded in historically rooted risk principles, and requiring proof of intoxication at the moment of possession (as Respondents effectively would) would collapse historically permissible prophylaxis into an unworkable mini-trial regime. To the extent Justice Gorsuch raises fair-notice/lenity concerns, those arguments go to statutory application and evidentiary sufficiency, and on this record—showing ongoing use close in time to possession—the as-applied burden is sufficiently tethered to the historically recognized impairment rationale.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that the historical record more clearly supports bans on being armed while actually intoxicated (or narrow habitual-drunkard regimes) and that § 922(g)(3) lacks the kind of individualized, surety-like process Rahimi discussed; that fair-notice/process concern is real and should cabin our decision. But Rahimi also makes clear, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, that Bruen does not require a Founding-era “twin”—the question is whether the modern restriction is comparably justified and comparably burdensome, and a temporary, condition-linked disarmament during ongoing unlawful use fits the historical principle that legislatures may separate arms from those whose substance condition predictably impairs judgment and heightens risk. I agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh that requiring proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession would effectively collapse a prophylactic rule into an unworkable impairment mini-trial that history does not demand. To accommodate Justice Gorsuch’s notice/separation-of-powers concerns, I would join an as-applied holding that hinges on a record of regular, contemporaneous unlawful use close in time to possession, leaving harder, more attenuated applications for future cases.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen, the government must identify a relevantly similar historical tradition, not a founding-era “twin,” and § 922(g)(3) can be upheld on narrow, as-applied grounds where the record shows ongoing unlawful use that implicates the historically recognized danger of armed impairment. As Rahimi confirms, legislatures may disarm individuals based on a demonstrated nexus to dangerousness consistent with historical analogues, and courts should not demand case-by-case dangerousness mini-trials that would undermine administrability and institutional legitimacy. Here, § 922(g)(3)’s temporary, conduct-linked restriction (limited to periods of being an “unlawful user” of controlled substances) fits within the tradition of restricting arms possession/use by those whose intoxication or habitual abuse makes gun possession unusually risky. I would reverse the Fifth Circuit and uphold § 922(g)(3) as applied to Hemani, leaving broader facial questions for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Bruen and Rahimi, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers Hemani’s possession, the Government must justify § 922(g)(3) by a historical tradition of firearm regulation with a relevantly similar “why” and “how.” The cited analogues—laws punishing carrying or firing while actively intoxicated and scattered “habitual drunkard” measures—target contemporaneous impairment or extreme incapacity, not a categorical, ongoing disarmament disability keyed to the modern federal label “controlled substance” irrespective of intoxication at the time of possession. Because § 922(g)(3)’s “unlawful user” prong operates as a broad status-based prohibition without a founding-era analogue of comparable breadth, it fails Bruen’s test as applied to Hemani. The Second Amendment does not permit Congress to impose this categorical ban absent proof of intoxication-at-possession or a historically grounded limiting principle comparable to the founding-era restrictions the Government invokes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3) bars firearm possession by anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance,” and that text reasonably reaches ongoing unlawful use without requiring proof of contemporaneous intoxication at the exact moment of possession. Under Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, the government need not produce a “historical twin”; it is enough to identify a relevantly similar tradition of disarming or restricting arms access for persons whose condition makes armed possession unusually dangerous, such as historical limits on the armed intoxicated and “habitual drunkards.” Rahimi confirms that status-linked disarmament fits within our tradition when it targets a demonstrated risk of violence and is appropriately bounded; § 922(g)(3), as applied to an ongoing unlawful drug user like Hemani, operates as a practical, temporary disqualification keyed to current unlawful use rather than a permanent deprivation. The Fifth Circuit’s demand for a near-identical founding-era analogue is inconsistent with Bruen’s allowance for analogous reasoning and would substantially disable an important law-enforcement tool aimed at preventing predictable, impairment-related gun violence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, § 922(g)(3) fits within a historical principle—reaffirmed in Rahimi—that legislatures may temporarily disarm categories of persons whose ongoing condition makes firearm possession unusually dangerous, even without a founding-era “twin.” The Government’s analogues (restrictions on the armed intoxicated and on “habitual drunkards”) support Congress’s judgment that regular unlawful drug use is a risk marker for dangerous armed behavior, and § 922(g)(3) is limited in duration to the period of unlawful use rather than imposing a lifetime ban. As applied to Hemani, the statute targets an unlawful user of controlled substances under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) without requiring a moment-of-possession intoxication showing, which would be impractical to administer and would undercut a prophylactic rule aimed at preventing foreseeable harm. Upholding the statute also advances fairness and public safety by protecting vulnerable communities disproportionately harmed by gun violence while preserving room for as-applied challenges where the Government cannot prove ongoing unlawful use.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, § 922(g)(3)’s temporary disarmament of persons who are “unlawful user[s] of…controlled substance[s]” is sufficiently analogous to historical regulations that restricted firearm possession or use by those whose intoxication or habitual abuse made armed activity unusually dangerous, even absent proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession. Read pragmatically and textually, § 922(g)(3) targets an ongoing condition of unlawful drug use closely connected to impairment and elevated risk, and it operates in a workable, status-linked way rather than requiring case-by-case dangerousness findings that would be difficult to administer. Rahimi reinforces that the historical inquiry looks for “relevantly similar” analogues and permits categorical restrictions keyed to risk-bearing conditions, so long as they are not a free-floating “dangerousness” blank check; here the analogue is anchored in the tradition of regulating armed intoxication/habitual intoxication and thus fits. As applied to Hemani, the statute permissibly reaches regular unlawful use because Congress may treat ongoing unlawful consumption of controlled substances as a disqualifying condition consistent with that tradition and with statutory coherence across § 922(g)’s disqualifying categories.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers Hemani’s conduct (possessing a firearm), the government must justify § 922(g)(3)’s disarmament rule by a relevantly similar historical tradition, and the best proffered analogues—laws restricting the armed while actually intoxicated or targeting “habitual drunkards”—do not establish a Founding-era tradition of disarming a person based on a general status of “unlawful user” when not shown to be intoxicated at the time of possession. Rahimi allows disarmament where history shows a principle of temporarily disarming those who have been found to pose a concrete threat (e.g., surety/analogous processes), but § 922(g)(3)’s “unlawful user” prong operates without an individualized judicial finding of dangerousness or contemporaneous impairment, making the fit too attenuated under Bruen’s analogical inquiry. The statute’s breadth, keyed to Congress’s controlled-substances classifications rather than historically recognized categories of incapacity or demonstrated danger, also raises serious separation-of-powers and fair-notice concerns in this criminal context, where the rule of lenity counsels against expanding historical analogues to sustain a categorical ban. As applied to Hemani under § 922(g)(3)’s “unlawful user” prong, the government has not carried its burden to show the regulation is consistent with the Nation’s history and tradition of firearm regulation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers the conduct, the government may justify a firearm restriction by showing a relevantly similar historical tradition, not a founding-era “twin.” Rahimi reinforces that legislatures have long been permitted to disarm categories of persons who present a special danger of misuse, and historical analogues like laws restricting arms use by the intoxicated and regulating “habitual drunkards” support Congress’s judgment in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) that ongoing unlawful drug use can pose heightened risks even when the defendant is not shown to be intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. As applied here, the prohibition is temporary and condition-linked (it turns on current unlawful use), making it practically workable and consistent with a historically grounded principle of disarming dangerous conditions rather than imposing an unbounded status disability. Given Rahimi’s allowance for categorical prohibitions grounded in dangerousness and Bruen’s analogical method, I would uphold § 922(g)(3) as applied to Hemani.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3)’s text targets a condition of ongoing unlawful drug use—“is an unlawful user of or addicted to”—rather than a single moment of intoxication, and the Second Amendment inquiry after Bruen asks whether the modern restriction is relevantly similar to historical regulations aimed at reducing the danger of armed impairment. Under Bruen and this Court’s clarification in United States v. Rahimi, the government need not produce a founding-era twin or demand individualized dangerousness findings in each case; it must identify a historical tradition of disarming persons whose status or condition makes firearm possession unusually dangerous, and laws addressing armed intoxication and “habitual drunkards” supply a sufficiently analogous principle. Hemani’s as-applied challenge fails because § 922(g)(3) is a temporary, conduct-linked disarmament tied to ongoing unlawful use, not a permanent, amorphous status ban, and it fits within the historical tradition of preventing armed misuse by those whose impaired judgment heightens risk. Precedent counsels methodological consistency with Rahimi’s level-of-generality approach and reinforces that categorical rules may be permissible where history reflects disarmament keyed to danger-producing conditions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, Congress may disarm persons whose ongoing condition or status is reasonably tied to heightened risk of dangerous firearm misuse, even absent proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession, so long as the modern law is comparably justified and comparably burdensome. Section 922(g)(3) is best understood as a temporary, condition-linked restriction aimed at preventing armed impairment and its practical consequences, and it fits within a historical tradition of regulating firearms in connection with intoxication and chronic substance abuse (e.g., restrictions targeting intoxicated use/carrying and "habitual drunkards") rather than requiring case-by-case judicial findings of dangerousness in every prosecution. Consistent with Rahimi, the Court should not demand a founding-era “twin” and should reject an administratively unworkable individualized-dangerousness regime that would undermine procedural fairness and uniform enforcement of § 922(g)(3). As applied to Hemani—charged under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3)’s “unlawful user” prong—the prohibition is constitutional because it targets contemporaneous, ongoing unlawful drug use that Congress reasonably determined correlates with elevated gun-violence risk, not a permanent ban untethered from conduct.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Amendment permits Congress to categorically prohibit firearm possession by a person who is an "unlawful user" of a controlled substance—even when the person is not shown to be intoxicated at the time of gun possession—under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) as applied to Ali Danial Hemani.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as interpreted under New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen’s historical-tradition test) and 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (prohibiting firearm possession by anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because the Second Amendment’s historical tradition allows disarming people whose ongoing condition or conduct makes them dangerous or untrustworthy with firearms; historical analogues include laws restricting arms possession or carrying by intoxicated persons and by "habitual drunkards," and modern drug-user prohibitions are a permissible translation of those principles to contemporary controlled substances. The government also emphasizes that the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively invalidates most applications of § 922(g)(3), creates and deepens a circuit split, and undermines an important, frequently used public-safety statute; it contends the statute is tailored/temporary in the sense that the prohibition tracks ongoing unlawful use and does not require individualized dangerousness adjudications for each defendant.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to him under Bruen because the government cannot identify sufficiently analogous Founding-era or Reconstruction-era traditions that disarm people merely for regular use of an unlawful substance when they are not intoxicated while possessing the firearm; at most, historical evidence supports disarming people who are actively intoxicated/using at the time of gun possession, or those whose condition rises to something like a "habitual drunkard" (i.e., impaired, dysfunctional, or demonstrably dangerous), not ordinary or episodic users. He maintains he is bringing an as-applied challenge focused on the mismatch between the statute’s breadth (covering many regular users) and the narrower historical tradition (aimed at actual intoxication or severe impairment), and he resists the government’s effort to characterize his argument as a de facto facial challenge.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va.; aff’d 4th Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best objection: the clearest historical analogues regulate carrying while actively intoxicated, and “habitual drunkard” measures are too thin to justify a broad, status-like prohibition untethered to contemporaneous impairment. But Rahimi matters here, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, because it confirms Bruen’s analogical inquiry tolerates category-based, preventive disarmament where the restriction tracks a historically grounded rationale aimed at a “special danger of misuse,” not a requirement of a Founding-era twin keyed to identical triggers. To respect that limit and avoid overreading history at too high a level of generality, I would uphold § 922(g)(3) only as applied on proof of ongoing, regular unlawful use sufficiently contemporaneous with the period of possession to demonstrate materially heightened risk, leaving marginal cases (e.g., remote or sporadic use) for future as-applied challenges. On that narrowed footing, the respondents’ mismatch critique loses force under my minimalist approach while preserving the statute’s temporally limited design and the Court’s institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed as-applied narrowing—requiring proof of “ongoing, regular unlawful use” contemporaneous with possession—cannot supply the historical tradition Bruen demands; it is a modern policy compromise that still lacks a Founding-era analogue for disarming based on status absent contemporaneous impairment. Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh rely on Rahimi’s statement that legislatures may disarm “categories” posing a “special danger of misuse,” but Rahimi still requires a historically grounded “why” and “how,” and the best proffered analogues regulate carrying while actively intoxicated or, at most, extreme habitual drunkenness—not a broad federal felony keyed to “unlawful user” status without proof the person was impaired while armed. Elevating a general risk principle (“drug users are dangerous”) to justify a categorical ban untethered to the moment of possession is precisely the level-of-generality move Bruen rejects. Because the Government’s analogues do not establish a well-settled tradition matching § 922(g)(3)’s means and scope as applied here, I see no originalist basis to change my vote.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Founding-era regulations most clearly targeted armed conduct during active intoxication, and that § 922(g)(3) cannot be justified by abstracting that into a free-floating “status” disability. But the statute’s own text—“unlawful user”—already cabins it to a present, ongoing condition, and Chief Justice Roberts is right that we can and should read the statute as applied to require proof of regular, contemporaneous unlawful use during the period of possession, avoiding the overbreadth concerns without rewriting the law into an “intoxicated-at-the-moment” rule. Rahimi, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, confirms that category-based, preventive disarmament can be consistent with the Second Amendment when tied to a historically grounded public-safety rationale, even absent individualized dangerousness trials in every case. On that narrower as-applied framing, the historical analogues to intoxication and habitual drunkenness are sufficiently similar in why and how—temporary disarmament keyed to continuing use presenting an elevated risk—to sustain this application.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to press that the cleanest Founding-era analogues are conduct-based (disarming while actively intoxicated), and that we cannot just relabel a narrow historical rule into a sweeping status disability. But under Bruen’s analogical inquiry—especially as Rahimi frames it—the question is relevant similarity in why/how, and legislatures may disarm a category posing a special danger of misuse without proving intoxication at the precise moment of possession, so long as the restriction is tied to a continuing condition predictive of impaired judgment. Chief Justice Roberts’s as-applied approach best answers the mismatch concerns by requiring proof of ongoing, regular unlawful use temporally proximate to possession, keeping § 922(g)(3) a limited preventive measure rather than a permanent deprivation. Requiring moment-of-possession intoxication would, as Justice Kagan notes, effectively rewrite the statute into an unworkable standard and undercut protections for communities most exposed to gun violence without any historical necessity to do so.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best objection—that the historical record most clearly targets being armed while actively intoxicated, and thus cannot justify § 922(g)(3) absent proof of impairment at the moment of possession. But under Bruen’s analogical inquiry as clarified by Rahimi, the question is whether the modern rule is “relevantly similar” in why and how; the tradition of regulating armed intoxication and habitual drunkards supports a risk-based principle of temporarily disarming those whose ongoing intoxicant use makes safe gun handling materially less reliable, not merely punishing past use. Chief Justice Roberts’s as-applied narrowing responds to the mismatch concern by requiring proof of current, regular unlawful use sufficiently contemporaneous with possession—avoiding both an unadministrable “intoxicated-at-the-moment” rewrite and an overbroad, status-like disability untethered from present risk. Rahimi (invoked by Roberts and Kavanaugh) matters here because it rejects any demand for a “historical twin” and confirms that categorical, preventive disarmament can be constitutional when keyed to a historically grounded rationale, which is what this narrowed application supplies.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed as-applied narrowing—requiring proof of ongoing, regular use temporally linked to possession—mitigates overbreadth concerns, but it does not supply the historically grounded analogue Bruen demands for § 922(g)(3)’s status-triggered felony disarmament absent proof of contemporaneous impairment or a surety-like, process-backed restraint. Rahimi’s language about disarming categories posing a “special danger of misuse,” as Justice Kavanaugh stresses, cannot be read at so high a level of generality that any risk proxy suffices; the Government still must show a tradition with a comparably tailored “why” and “how,” and the intoxication/habitual-drunkard materials regulate being armed while drunk or demonstrably incapacitated, not mere unlawful use untethered to the moment of possession. Justice Alito’s analogy to “temporary disarmament keyed to continuing use” assumes what history must prove, because the historical mechanisms were narrower and often conduct-based rather than a sweeping federal prohibition. Administrability and public-safety policy, even when weighty as Justice Sotomayor argues, cannot replace the missing historical fit where the Second Amendment’s text presumptively covers the conduct.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch raise the hardest point: the best Founding-era analogues target carrying while actively intoxicated, not a broader disability pegged to “unlawful user” status without proof of impairment at the precise moment of possession. But under Bruen’s analogical method as clarified by Rahimi, the question is whether the modern law is relevantly similar in why and how, and Rahimi recognizes a tradition of preventive, category-based restrictions aimed at those with probable grounds to fear misuse—not requiring a bespoke dangerousness trial in every case. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow as-applied framing addresses the mismatch concern by demanding proof of ongoing, regular unlawful use sufficiently contemporaneous with possession to function as a temporary, risk-based translation of intoxication/habitual-drunkard restrictions, rather than a lifetime status ban. On that understanding, the Respondents’ position would effectively rewrite § 922(g)(3) into an “intoxicated-at-the-moment” rule that history does not clearly compel and that would undermine the statute’s workable, temporally limited design.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the best objection: the most concrete historical analogues regulate armed conduct while actively intoxicated, and translating that into a broader disability risks converting a conduct rule into a status ban. But under Bruen’s analogical method—as Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, and as Rahimi confirms—the question is relevant similarity in why/how, and history supports temporarily disarming persons whose ongoing condition predictably heightens the risk of dangerous misuse, even without a “historical twin” or an individualized dangerousness proceeding in every case. The textual limitation to current “unlawful user[s]” matters: on the Chief Justice’s as-applied narrowing (requiring proof of regular, ongoing unlawful use contemporaneous with the possession period), the statute operates as a temporally bounded, risk-tethered restriction rather than a permanent status punishment. Because that approach answers the overbreadth concern without rewriting § 922(g)(3) into an intoxication-at-the-moment requirement, I do not see the respondents’ history mismatch as sufficient to overcome the Government’s showing here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch rightly press that the clearest historical analogues regulate armed conduct during active intoxication, and that a purely status-based, noncontemporaneous ban would be a poor fit under Bruen’s “why/how” test. But I am persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s framing that we can read § 922(g)(3) as applied here to require proof of ongoing, regular unlawful use temporally linked to the period of possession, which makes the law function as a risk-based, time-limited disarmament rather than an abstract status disability. Rahimi matters because it rejects the premise that the Second Amendment demands individualized dangerousness adjudications in every case and instead allows historically grounded category-based prevention where the rationale is to reduce predictable misuse. On this record of current, sustained unlawful use, the historical tradition of disarming those whose intoxicant use makes firearm handling foreseeably unreliable is “relevantly similar” enough that Bruen does not compel invalidation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s historical-tradition framework, § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied where the Government proves ongoing unlawful use that renders firearm possession materially more dangerous, a principle consistent with historical restrictions on armed intoxication and disarmament of those deemed dangerous or untrustworthy. Rahimi confirms that legislatures may disarm “categories of persons” who “present a special danger of misuse” without requiring case-by-case dangerousness trials in every prosecution, so long as the restriction tracks a historically grounded rationale. To avoid unnecessary disruption and preserve institutional legitimacy, I would reverse on narrow grounds: uphold § 922(g)(3) as applied to Hemani based on proof of contemporaneous, regular unlawful use tied to gun possession, without deciding broader facial questions about the statute’s outer reach. This approach respects precedent while leaving room for future as-applied challenges where the nexus between drug use and dangerousness is materially weaker.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers ordinary possession of a firearm, so under Bruen the Government must identify a well-established historical analogue for disarming a person based solely on status as an “unlawful user” absent intoxication at the time of possession. The historical record the Government invokes—laws against carrying while intoxicated and some regulations aimed at “habitual drunkards”—at most supports restricting gun use during active intoxication or in cases of severe, demonstrable impairment, not a categorical disability triggered by regular but temporally distinct drug use. Section 922(g)(3), as applied to Hemani under the “unlawful user” prong, therefore lacks the required historical tradition and operates as an impermissible status-based ban untethered to the Founding-era understanding of who may be disarmed. Rahimi’s discussion of historically grounded, targeted measures (e.g., surety-type restrictions) underscores that broad, categorical disarmament requires a closer historical match than the Government has shown here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3)’s text targets an ongoing condition—being an “unlawful user” of controlled substances—rather than a momentary act, and Congress may treat that continuing unlawful use as a proxy for impaired judgment and heightened risk with firearms. Under Bruen’s historical-tradition framework, the government’s analogues to regulations disarming the intoxicated and “habitual drunkards” are sufficiently comparable in justification (preventing gun possession by those whose substance use makes them dangerous or unreliable) and burden (a temporary disarmament that tracks ongoing use rather than permanent deprivation). Rahimi reinforces that the Second Amendment permits disarmament measures aimed at protecting public safety based on historically grounded principles, and it would have severe practical consequences for law enforcement and public safety to require individualized dangerousness findings in each § 922(g)(3) case. Hemani’s narrowing proposal would convert a workable categorical rule into an administrability problem that undermines a core federal firearms prohibition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within the Second Amendment’s historical tradition, as operationalized in Bruen, of disarming categories of persons whose ongoing condition or conduct makes firearm possession especially risky—an approach this Court reaffirmed in Rahimi when it recognized that legislatures may prohibit gun possession by categories presenting a “special danger of misuse.” The historical analogues need not be a perfect match; regulations targeting intoxication and habitual drunkenness reflect the same principle that firearms may be withheld from those whose substance use predictably impairs judgment and elevates risk even if intoxication is not proved at the precise moment of possession. Congress’s choice of a categorical, temporally limited disability keyed to ongoing “unlawful use” (rather than permanent disarmament) is a practical, administrable safeguard that prevents avoidable violence and protects vulnerable communities without requiring case-by-case dangerousness trials for every defendant. On this record, invalidating § 922(g)(3) as applied would unduly hamstring a core public-safety statute and contradict Rahimi’s rejection of demanding individualized dangerousness determinations as a constitutional prerequisite for disarmament regimes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, the question is whether § 922(g)(3)’s application to Hemani fits within the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, allowing “relevantly similar” analogues rather than a dead-ringer match. As Rahimi emphasized, the Second Amendment does not bar Congress from disarming “categories of persons” who “present a special danger of misuse,” and history reflects a sustained tradition of restricting access to arms for persons whose ongoing intoxication-related condition (e.g., habitual drunkards) undermines safe, responsible gun use—an analogue Congress could reasonably translate to ongoing unlawful use of controlled substances. Given § 922(g)(3)’s text limiting the ban to a current “unlawful user” (not past use) and its administrable, workably categorical nature, I would uphold the statute as applied here without requiring proof of contemporaneous intoxication at the moment of possession. This approach preserves statutory coherence within § 922(g) and aligns with Bruen’s instruction that modern regulations may address persistent risks using historically grounded principles.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Bruen holds that once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers an individual’s conduct, the Government must justify 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) by identifying a “well-established and representative” historical analogue with a sufficiently similar “why” and “how.” 142 S. Ct. at 2126, 2133. Rahimi reaffirms that the Government need not supply a “historical twin,” but it must point to a tradition that justifies disarmament on comparable grounds and by comparable means, not by converting a narrow, conduct-based rule (disarming the actively intoxicated) into a broad, status-based prohibition (disarming anyone deemed an “unlawful user” absent contemporaneous impairment). 602 U.S. ___, at 681. As applied to Hemani—prosecuted only under the “unlawful user” prong, without proof of intoxication while possessing the firearm—the cited intoxication and “habitual drunkard” laws do not supply the requisite analogue, and the mismatch must be resolved in favor of the individual right the Constitution protects.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, § 922(g)(3)’s temporary disarmament of persons who are ongoing “unlawful user[s]” of controlled substances fits within a historical tradition of keeping arms from categories of persons viewed as posing a special risk of misuse—most closely reflected in regulations targeting intoxicated carriers and “habitual drunkards.” Rahimi reinforces that the Second Amendment tolerates preventive, category-based restrictions aimed at those with a “probable ground to suspect of future misbehavior,” and it does not require individualized dangerousness determinations in every case. As applied here, Congress could reasonably treat ongoing unlawful drug use as an intoxicating condition akin to historical analogues, and a categorical rule is practically workable compared to case-by-case intoxication proof at the moment of possession. Given the statute’s limiting feature—coverage tied to current, ongoing unlawful use rather than a permanent status—§ 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied to Hemani.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Hemani’s conduct—possessing a firearm—falls within the Second Amendment’s plain text, so under Bruen the Government must show § 922(g)(3)’s application is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. Reading Bruen and Rahimi at the proper level of generality, the relevant tradition permits legislatures to impose categorical, status-based disarmament where an ongoing condition reliably correlates with dangerousness or untrustworthiness, and historical restrictions on armed intoxication and on “habitual drunkards” supply a sufficiently analogous principle even when the person is not intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. Section 922(g)(3) is also temporally linked to ongoing unlawful use (not a permanent disability), which further supports its fit with the historical practice of disarming those whose continuing condition poses heightened risk. Although the statute may sweep more broadly than some historical rules, Bruen does not demand a “historical twin,” and precedent permits reasonable translation of established principles to modern controlled substances.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, § 922(g)(3)’s temporary disarmament of an “unlawful user” fits within the Second Amendment’s historically recognized authority to restrict firearm access for persons whose ongoing condition or conduct makes gun possession unusually dangerous, even if the government cannot prove contemporaneous intoxication at the moment of possession. Under Bruen’s analogical approach, historical restrictions on carrying/possessing arms while intoxicated and on “habitual drunkards” are relevantly similar in purpose and fit, and Rahimi confirms that legislatures may employ categorical rules aimed at preventing firearm misuse when tied to a demonstrated risk rationale rather than punishing status alone. Procedurally, requiring individualized dangerousness adjudications in every § 922(g)(3) case would undermine administrability and consistent enforcement of a core public-safety measure, and Congress reasonably linked ongoing unlawful controlled-substance use to impaired judgment and heightened risk. The Fifth Circuit’s contrary approach functionally collapses § 922(g)(3) into only “intoxicated-at-the-moment” cases, which is too cramped a reading of historical tradition and too dismissive of practical consequences for public safety.
